office.title: Indiana State Representative
office.summary: Members of the Indiana House of Representatives write and vote on state laws as part of the Indiana General Assembly. The House has 100 members, each representing one district for a two-year term [1].
duties: Introduces and votes on state legislation as one of the two chambers of the Indiana General Assembly [1].
Must be at least 21 years old when taking office and have lived in the district for at least a year [1].

incumbent.name: Lorissa Sweet
incumbent.summary: Lorissa Sweet, a Wabash small-business owner and former Wabash County councilwoman, has represented House District 50 since 2022 [3, 4]. She serves on the Agriculture and Rural Development; Family, Children and Human Affairs; and Local Government committees [3].
record: Committees: Agriculture and Rural Development; Family, Children and Human Affairs; Local Government [3]. 2026 interim: Interim Study Committee on Government [5].

Feb. 2023: Offered a state budget amendment barring state funding for Indiana University's Kinsey Institute, which the House approved 53-34 [6]. WFYI reported she repeated allegations about founder Alfred Kinsey and claimed, without proof, that the institute and IU shelter sexual predators; Rep. Matt Pierce (D-Bloomington) said it angered him "when people's good names are sullied and libeled from this floor" [6].

2024 session: Authored HB 1286, which would have replaced voting machines and electronic poll books with hand-marked, hand-counted paper ballots; it was assigned to the House Elections and Apportionment Committee [7].

2025 session: Co-authored HB 1413, creating a grant fund for the Indiana State Police to clear a backlog of about 600 untested rape kits, which passed the House unanimously [8]; co-sponsored a law making it a crime to use or sell radio-frequency jamming devices, ceremonially signed in August 2025 [9].

April 10, 2025: Voted yes when the House passed SEA 1, the 2025 property-tax law, 65-29 [10]. April 25, 2025: Was excused and did not vote on the 2025 state budget conference report (HEA 1001), adopted 66-27 [11].

Dec. 5, 2025: Voted yes on HB 1032, the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which passed the House 57-41 [12]. In January 2026 she filed HB 1166, an elections bill that was referred to committee with no further action recorded [13].

race_context: House District 50 covers all of Huntington County and portions of Miami, Wabash and Wells counties, according to the House Republican caucus [3].
Sweet was first elected in 2022, succeeding Dan Leonard, and won re-election in 2024 with 76.9% of the vote [4, 14].
Sweet and Democrat Pepper Snyder were the only candidates listed in their parties' May 5, 2026 primaries [14]; both are on the November ballot [2].

Key differences: Snyder opposes expanding private-school vouchers, would eliminate sales tax on residential utility bills and supports a regulated adult cannabis market [15]; Sweet's campaign emphasizes individual liberty, gun rights, limited government and opposition to abortion [16], and she voted for SEA 1 and HB 1032 [10, 12].
No debate or forum for this race was found.

candidates.summary: Lorissa Sweet is the Republican incumbent, first elected in 2022 [3]. Her legislative work has included election administration, the 2023 Kinsey Institute funding amendment and public-safety bills [7, 6, 8].
background: Owns Sweet Grooms, a pet grooming business opened in 2009, and Sweet Occasions LLC, a wedding decor rental business started in 2021; lives in Wabash; holds a Purdue University degree in animal agribusiness [3].
Served on the Wabash County Council from 2016 until joining the House [3, 4].
path_to_ballot: Unopposed in the May 5, 2026 Republican primary [14].

items: Said of her 2024 paper-ballot bill: "Returning to hand-counted ballots will return us to the basics of voting and increase public confidence in our system" [7]. Voted for HB 1032 (2025 congressional redistricting) [12].
Said of HB 1413: "Due to limited resources, a backlog of untested rape kits has accumulated," and a dedicated fund would help ensure "violent criminals are held accountable" [8].
Campaign site: "I will not compromise when it comes to defending your Constitutional right to bear arms" [16].
On her 2023 Kinsey amendment: "We, as the governing body, need to put limits on the access to tax dollars we allow Indiana University to garner" [6].
Campaign site: "It is past time to reign in government overreach, unconstitutional edicts, and mandates" [16].

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. No statements by Sweet about Snyder were found.
plans: On her 2026 interim committee: said study committees let lawmakers "take a deep dive into issues that impact constituents" ahead of the next session [5].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or fundraising figures were found.
gaps: No candidate survey responses, interviews or 2026 campaign coverage were found.
Final outcome of HB 1413 (2025) not confirmed; the subject and outcome of HB 1166 (2026) beyond committee referral not found.
Search snippets list other 2026 bills by Sweet (HB 1304 on vintage-vehicle titles, HB 1295 on hospital disclosures) and a resolution honoring a national prayer event; not verified.
Search snippets say a 2023 Herald-Times article reported IU's president condemned the defunding; not verified.

candidates.summary: Pepper Snyder is a Huntington County resident who spent more than 13 years with the state's Family and Social Services Administration, including as a fraud investigator [17, 18]. Her campaign focuses on public school funding, utility costs, rural health care, child care and data-center tax policy [15].
background: Worked more than 13 years for the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration as an eligibility specialist, fraud investigator and state eligibility manager [17]; her campaign says she supervised and investigated food stamp and Medicaid fraud [18].
Lives in Huntington County; Seeger High School graduate; her husband is a U.S. Army infantry veteran [18].
A Pepper Snyder of Huntington was the Libertarian Party's 2016 nominee for Indiana's 3rd Congressional District [19, 14].
path_to_ballot: The only Democrat listed in the May 5, 2026 primary [14].

items: Would "Protect public school funding instead of continuing to expand taxpayer-funded private-school vouchers" [15].
Would eliminate the sales tax on residential utility bills and oppose rate hikes: "If billion-dollar data centers get the break, Hoosier families should too" [15].
Says she would "Make billion-dollar data centers pay their fair share, protect local control" and keep large developments from polluting land, water or air [15].
Would "Fight to keep hospitals, maternity care, pediatric care and other essential health services available close to home" [15].
Supports a child care tax credit for working families and full funding of CCDF vouchers [15].
Supports a regulated, adult-only cannabis market, saying revenue could fund schools, roads and mental health services and "provide property tax relief" [15].

on_incumbent: Her campaign does not name Sweet; it criticizes the Republican supermajority's record, including data-center tax breaks and child care voucher cuts, and says "It's time for representation that puts Hoosiers before corporations" [17].
plans: Says her goal is "making Indiana affordable again" for working families, seniors and the next generation [18].
endorsements_finance: Her campaign lists an endorsement from Veterans for Indiana [20].
gaps: No independent news coverage of Snyder's 2026 campaign was found.
Her campaign's statistical claims about the legislature's record (e.g., coverage losses for children, data-center tax-break totals) were not independently checked.
Whether she is the same person as the 2016 Libertarian congressional nominee is reported by Wikipedia but not confirmed by her campaign.
A campaign newsletter found in search snippets says she has outraised Sweet; not verified. No campaign finance data found.
